newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl doggedly optimistic in face of tough problems.
newsitem.headline: Kohl doggedly optimistic in face of tough problems.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl displayed dogged optimism on Thursday in the face of an array of challenges including mounting economic woes in Germany, fear of a European Union currency, Russian resistance to NATO expansion and speculation about his leadership.

Kohl's New Year press conference coincided with news that unemployment in Germany rose in December to a seasonally adjusted post-war record of 4.156 million, a level he called "completely unacceptable", and that the economy had stagnated last quarter.

Germany's 1996 budget deficit also rose to 3.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), casting doubt on Bonn's ability to reach the three percent ceiling this year to qualify for Kohl's flagship project of an EU single currency.
But the chancellor told reporters: "If I look at Germany and feel pessimistic, I have to ask what country we're living in... I can't see why I should be pessimistic."
Underpinning prospects for economic recovery were low interest rates, price stability, a positive global economic outlook and moderate wage settlements, Kohl said.
Economists said the latest figures showed Germany trapped in a vicious circle of mounting unemployment and weak growth.
The 66-year-old chancellor, who faces a general election late next year, conceded that an economic upturn did not necessarily mean more jobs.
He said his goal of halving dole queues by the year 2000 would be difficult but not impossible and offered to chair a jobs summit of unions and employers.

But trade union federation chairman Dieter Schulte said such talks were unlikely to succeed where a similar attempt failed a year ago, because Bonn lacked the courage to admit its policies were swelling the ranks of the unemployed.

Despite Kohl's efforts to introduce a European single currency, a poll in the newspaper Handelsblatt said 44 percent of Germans would oppose it in a hypothetical referendum while 43 percent were in favour.

Kohl dismissed the idea of a referendum, which German law does not allow for. He told reporters: "I am confident that when...people have all the information, we will get a clear majority of the population for the euro."
He displayed similar confidence on Germany's chief foreign policy problem -- Russia's opposition to an extension of NATO into eastern Europe, taking in many of Germany's neighbours.
German is playing a key role, insisting Moscow cannot have a veto over NATO enlargement but arguing strongly that Russia must play a well-defined role in Europe's security architecture.
Kohl, who visited President Boris Yeltsin last Saturday, said he had concrete ideas for convincing Moscow to accept NATO expansion and was optimistic agreement could be reached.
"I am convinced that...we will find a reasonable balance (of interests) and there is a possibility to implement this NATO expansion into the east together," he said.
Kohl also said Germany was playing a substantial role in Middle East peace efforts, albeit behind the scenes, and that details of this would become clearer in the next few weeks.

The veteran chancellor has also come under pressure from an unexpected quarter since his loyal crown prince Wolfgang Schaeuble told a magazine that he would be tempted to take over as chancellor one day.

Editorial writers leapt on this as a carefully judged sign that Kohl might step aside in frustration at growing unemployment, to make way for a grand coalition with the opposition Social Democrats under Schaeuble, who is now parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats.
But Kohl declined to be drawn on how long he planned to stay in office.
"I do feel temptations, even at my age," he joked. "But I am not tempted to answer your question whether I will run or not."
